For a copy of the draft of an immigration treaty, which was presented to the Chinese minister on January 17, 1944. and referred to by the Right Honourable the Prime Minister in his statement to the house on April 17, 1944, at page 2126.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Comox-Albemi will recognize that his motion involves an important question of principle, that principle being that the privilege of privacy must be granted to exchanges of views between negotiating countries. Perhaps I -might say a word to the house on this matter of the negotiation of treaties.
Hon. members will realize that international treaties and agreements require a thorough and frank exchange of views between the parties involved. In some eases it is possible, after a certain fundamental stage of agreement has been reached, and especially when the treaty is a multilateral one, for the final modifications and expressions of view to be made at conferences which are open and public. However, the general principle is recognized in all countries and is, I think, of basic importance in international relations, that exchanges of views between countries in the course of negotiation of an agreement should not be made public by either party. It is obvious that the fear of misunderstanding, and the necessity of defending publicly any expression of view v'hieh might be only a tentative one set forth to explore all possibilities, would make it impossible for governments or their representatives to express themselves freely and frankly if they had to consider the possibility of publicity being given to their every word and proposal. Such a situation would render virtually impossible the negotiation of agreements and understandings between countries.
Did not the Prime Minister make it a public document when he alluded to it in the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. I alluded to the fact that a treaty was being negotiated, but beyond mentioning the subject, I did not disclose any of the terms of the treaty.

Mr. ILSLEY.: Mr. Speaker, this raises an important question which has been dealt with on several occasions. It is not regarded as being in the public interest to disclose the names of individual recipients of subsidies. The reasons for this position have been given by me in the house on at least two occasions.
I find that on April 17, 1944, an answer to a question by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) contains this:
A statement of government policy in connection with revealing the names of applicants or recipients of subsidy appears on page 2719 of Hansard for May 14, 1943.
One ground for the rule which has been adopted is that to give the subsidies paid to recipients reveals to importers the business of their competitors, and gives them information as to the amount and type of business being done.
Dropped.
Have there not been instances where similar questions have been answered by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I am practically sure that there has never been such an instance. The position was very carefully considered in the spring of 1942 and again in the spring of 1943. It was stated in the house at the time, without any exception being taken to it, so far as I know.

It seems to me that this principle should be clarified, because it involves the payment out of public moneys to individuals. It is the duty of the house to see to it that all such moneys are scrutinized in parliament. The principle which has been followed is a dangerous one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I admit the difficulty.
Generally speaking it has a salutary effect on the whole public service if it is realized that any amounts, payments for which are authorized, are subject to review by parliament. One has to weigh that advantage against the disadvantage of making available to competitors the current business of those about whom the information is sought. The effect would be to make available to importers the current business of their competitors. We thought it would be best not to give this information. The department thought it could be given later in another way. If the hon. member will look at the debates on the subject he will see that that point is considered. I must say however that I do not regard it, nor does the government regard it, as in the public interest to give information which would tell importers of the particular commodities, the exact amounts, and the extent and type of business done by their competitors.
At the present time practically every grocery store in Canada is pushing the sale of grapefruit juice in gallon cans. I believe the public should know whether a subsidy is being paid, and to whom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, well; there is no objection to that. I will give the information as to whether a subsidy is being paid, with the basis upon which it is being paid. The only thing I would object to is giving a list of the names of importers, and the amount each one gets. It would be on the same basis to everyone.
Would there be any difficulty in the minister's tabling that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
And after that, would there be any harm in showing me privately to whom these are paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

In reply to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, may I say that in addition to the social and other legislation already on the order paper and the usual financial measures, the following measures, most of which were forecast in the speech from the throne, have still to be introduced. There will be the Bank Act amending bill and a measure respecting the Quebec Savings Bank. There will be ancillary legislation to provide for credits for agriculture, and a measure for the insurance or guarantee of export credits. There will be national housing legislation, and a measure to provide for family allowances. There will be legislation to provide for a floor under farm prices, and legislation respecting administrative machinery for the disposal of surplus w'ar assets. There will be an act to amend the Aeronautics Act to provide for the establishment of an air transport board with consequential amendments to the Transport Act. There will be an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act to provide for the exercise of the franchise by members of the armed forces. There will be

an amendment to the Civil Service Superannuation Act. There will also be any measures to supplement the existing rehabilitation programme, including war service gratuities and an amendment to the Veterans' Land Act. There will be amendments to the Naval Service Act, and possible amendments to the criminal code. There will also be such legislation as may result from reports of committees.
*^s indicated in the speech from the throne it is anticipated that there will be measures respecting health insurance and contributory old age pensions. In some particulars this legislation will depend upon the degree to which agreement can be reached with the provinces. Should the proposed treaty with China, which I mentioned on Monday last, be concluded before the end of the session, there wiH be a measure to amend the Chinese Immigration Act. There is alwnys the possibility that some situations may arise while parliament is still in session which will require the bringing in of additional legislation. I would not wish the government to be bound verbatim, et literatim by the statement I have just made, but I have tried to indicate to the house as fully as possible the legislation which, so far as I can see, at the moment it is proposed to have introduced at this session.

May I make one suggestion to the Prime Minister with respect to the legislative programme? I think the house is cognizant of the amount of legislation yet to be dealt with in addition to war measures of a financial character. Perhaps the Prime Minister would be good enough to hold a conference with the government leader in the other house with the idea of having initiated in the other house such of the legislation he has mentioned as may be so dealt with. With that arrangement and with the help of committees some of the burden of legislating which falls upon this house might be diverted to the other house and we would thus have a somewhat better balance as between both houses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that I have had several conferences with the leader of the government in the Senate and he himself has brought forward the very question my hon. friend has just raised. The difficulty is that at a time of war most of the legislation is in the form of measures financial in character and most of them of necessity must be introduced in the Commons in the first instance. I mentioned an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act to provide for the exercise of the franchise by members of the armed forces. At first glance

Prime Ministers' Conference
this might seem to be legislation that might be initiated in the Senate, but hon. members will realize that it pertains to representation in the Commons and for that reason the measure could not very well be taken up there in the first instance.
The leader of the government in the Senate has in mind asking the members of that house to consider in committee some phases or aspects of the bills that will be before the Commons so that when these measures do reach the Senate the members of that honourable body will have more or less covered the ground which might otherwise have to be covered in lengthy debate. In this way it may be possible to have consideration of some of the measures carried on more or less simultaneously in both houses. I assure my hon. friend that the government is desirous of having as much of the existing programme initiated in the Senate as may be advisable and possible, but the exceptional character of a war session is. something which lies beyond the control of both houses.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Prime Minister a question based on the probability that he will be leaving shortly for the conference of prime ministers in Great Britain. I am sure that the entire house wishes him godspeed, a safe journey there, a profitable conference, and a safe return. While he is away no doubt he will be called upon to make exceedingly important pronouncements and perhaps commitments. My question is this. Has he considered the advisability of calling into conference before leaving for Great Britain the leaders of the various parties and groups in parliament in order that he may ascertain the attitude of the entire body of parliament upon the problems which will have to be dealt with at the conference?

I would reply to him that the government has responsibility, as he is aware, for whatever is done in the name of the government either in this house
or elsewhere, and having that responsibility the government has to be the judge of the best method of proceeding in these matters. I hope that I am familiar enough with the views of the members of all groups in this house to be able to express, I trust quite sincerely and intelligently, any point of view that it may be desirable to have expressed on their behalf, but I have not thought it would be necessary to have any meeting of the kind which my hon. friend has just mentioned before attempting to deal with the proceedings of the conference. What will be discussed at the conference-I should call it rather a meeting of the prime ministers of the nations of the British commonwealth because it is not to be a conference in the sense in which that term is generally used-will depend largely on the questions that may come up at the meetings. No doubt there will be many subjects discussed, some of which I am already aware of, and others which I shall not know about until I am present.
May I say to my hon. friend that I thank him very warmly for the good wishes he has extended to me, and I thank hon. members of the house for the kind manner in which they have received the hon. member's expression of those good wishes. I shall endeavour as best I can not to disappoint any hopes or expectations which hon. members may be kind enough to cherish, with respect to a consideration of the matters to be taken up in London.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, April 21, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Departmental administration, $90,907.

Will the Minister of National War Services make a general statement? We have no break-down before us.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Mr. Chairman, on Friday last towards the end of the sitting I was giving information in reply to questions put to me regarding specific operations of the Department of National War Services. I would ask the indulgence of the committee in order that I may give some further information which I suggest will be found interesting to the house and the country at large.
The men and the women of the Canadian armed forces have not been forgotten in an' important matter, and by that I mean their continued education. From the very beginning of the war an educational movement was started, and that has increased as the years have gone by. I am satisfied that an excellent job is being done in that direction.

Mr. Chairman, what the minister is trying to bring before the committee is a matter of great importance and of great moment, but I am unable to hear him because of the noise that is going on in the chamber. In order to help him, so that his voice will remain intact during the afternoon and evening sittings, I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, please to call the committee to order and see that some semblance of order is kept while the minister is making his statement.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Mr. Chairman, my voice being in, its present state I am truly indebted to the leader of the opposition. I have some notes, and while they are lengthy I do believe they are worthy of putting on the record so that they may be read by the citizens of Canada at large.
Educational services for all branches of the armed forces were initiated in 1939 by the Canadian Legion under the authority of the Departments of National Defence, now three departments. The intention at that time was

to make available adequate educational facilities of a constructive nature to occupy idle time, which does form a considerable part of military life at different intervals, and eventually during the pre-demobilization period. The services were designed with three objectives in mind: first, that service personnel might become more efficient fighting men; second, that interrupted or deferred studies resulting from service might be continued; and third, that service personnel might prepare themselves whilst in service for civil reestablishment.
As the work developed, practical courses were established to meet the purely voluntary demands of service personnel. Later, the needs of additional educational facilities as part of military training were recognized by the three armed services. As an example, it became necessary to teach mathematics and other necessary subjects for which adequate facilities were not available within the services.
Canadian Legion Educational Services, having become established and capable of providing the necessary facilities for educating armed personnel proceeded to fit men in this respect for their military duties. The next step was for the three armed services themselves to develop in service organizations a knowledge of how to coordinate and integrate the educational facilities available through the Canadian Legion. Accordingly, the navy made use of its existing directorate of education, the army established its directorate of education in 1943, and the air force appointed educational officers in 1942. As a result of the establishment of these educational controls within the three services, all educational requirements, both for inservice training and extra-service training, are now' initiated by these officers, and required services-text books, libraries, supplies and instructors-are supplied through and by the Canadian Legion.
Because of the wide variation in school standards across Canada and because of the many different types of textbooks used in the autonomous provincial Bystems, it was found necessary to prepare numerous sets of academic, technical and vocational courses, ranging from the subjects on the lower level of the elementary school to those of the senior matriculation level. The collaboration of the provincial departments of education, extension departments of the universities, the Canada and Newfoundland educational association and other educational authorities was obviously necessary and was obtained by the Canadian Legion through its committee on education. Through its collaboration, the services now provide an interprovincial

War Appropriation-War Services
bilingual school system for the personnel of the fighting forces in which each registered student may obtain regular school credit. The core of the system provides sixty-seven specially prepared courses set out in text books which can be used in both oral courses and correspondence courses. This list includes certain special courses prepared at the request of the service authorities to assist in the more rapid preparation of service personnel in becoming efficient members of the fighting forces. One example of the manner in which such special courses have assisted in the training of personnel is that of the pre-aircrew courses. When the Royal Canadian Air Force had exhausted the supply of young men with sufficient academic education to take advantage of flying training, the Canadian Legion Educational Services were requested to provide pre-aircrew courses to bring ground crew personnel up to the required standards. To date, 12,603 students have taken advantage of pre-aircrew English, 21,428 have studied pre-aircrew mathematics and 15,430 have studied pre-aircrew science. This has materially assisted the R.C.A.F. in maintaining a steady flow of aircrew.
It is a matter of note, I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that through these operations, through the activities of the Canadian Legion Educational Services, there has been brought about, for the first time so far as I know, a system of teaching, or a school system if you like, which is identical in the nine provinces of Canada. That has been possible only because of the very fine cooperation which the several provinces without exception have afforded this plan.
Total voluntary registrations for correspondence courses using these text booklets as at March 31, 1944, was 129,361. During the past tw'o years the total number of papers corrected has been 210,197. Many of the students are not interested in academic credit, but study in preparation for promotion within the services, and consequently courses are dropped when the immediate aim is achieved.

Has the minister any comparison between those two years, as to whether there has been a substantial increase over the preceding year, so that we can see if there has been a progressive increase in the value of these courses? I do not want to interrupt.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I had intended to speak of that later on in my comments. That comes really at the end of my remarks on this subject. I think I can satisfy the hon gentleman on that.
Despite this fact, some 58 per cent are classified at present as active students working to complete courses. When consideration is given to the difficulties under which service personnel have to study, this average appears to be extremely good. Courses most in demand are mathematics, which includes trigonometry and practical courses designed especially for the army and the air force; conversation Anglaise; pilotage and elementary navigation; and series of technical, vocational and agricultural courses. Requirements for class instruction are provided in each military district or command of the R.C.A.F. by regional committees of the Canadian Legion Education Services, under the chairmanship of outstanding educationalists who serve in a voluntary capacity.
The following are the chairmen at the moment of these several regional committees in Canada and Newfoundland: Dr. G. M. Shrum, University of British Columbia; Professor Donald Cameron, University of Alberta; Dr. J. S. Thomson, President of the University , of Saskatchewan; Dr. Sidney Smith, President . of the University of Manitoba; Dr. M. K. Inman, Director of Extension, University of Western Ontario; Dr. W. J. Dunlop, Director of Extension, University of Toronto; Mr. Robert Westwater, Inspector of Ottawa Schools; Dr. J. C. Bonar, of the Canadian Pacific Railways; Mr. Victor Dore, Superintendent of Education, province of Quebec; Dr. N. MacKenzie, President of the University of New Brunswick; Dr. Henry F. Munro, Superintendent of Education, province of Nova Scotia; Honourable J. W. Jones, Premier of the province of Prince Edward Island; Dr.
A. G. Hatcher, President of Memorial College, Newfoundland.
On these regional committees are representatives of the director of education of the three armed services, department of education, teachers' societies, local school boards, auxiliary service officers, the provincial departments of agriculture, fisheries, mines and forestry. They are responsible for all operations within their respective areas. As will be seen, the planning has been central, with provincial consent; whereas the operations are in a sense decentralized; their geographical designations may rightly be compared with the several military districts.

Is there a central
advisory committee?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes. I am coming to that. Under this arrangement, from the time of inception until December 31, 1943, some 7,670 classes have been conducted with an

War Appropriation-War Services
enrolment of 196,849 men and women. Classes for in-service training are conducted entirely by the service authorities, but in many cases text booklets for such ordinarily are provided by Canadian Legion Educational Services, the only source really from which such textbooks can be had. Slightly over 275,000 text booklets have been supplied at the request of the three services. Many instructors for classes in extra-service studies give their services voluntarily. In cases where payment is required, local rates of remuneration prevail. Such rates vary, because of location and difficulty of subject, ranging from about S3 to $5 for class sessions of two hours. Instructors' fees for correspondence courses average around forty cents per paper which is marked, and the student is individually instructed in respect to errors. Personnel engaged in correspondence instruction are drawn from the ranks of professional correspondence instructors accredited by the provincial departments of education.
There are handicraft and art classes carried out by the Legion and the other auxiliary services. Classes are provided by regional committees at the request of the armed service as and when need arises. These classes embrace such fields of interest as handicrafts, arts, household science and pre-discharge classes leading to rehabilitation. Crafts and arts of special interest are: leather, wood and metal work, knitting and needlepoint, weaving, photography, sketching and painting. Handicraft and arts programmes were initiated about November, 1943, and interest in such courses developed rapidly. For example, during the four months following inception 30,863 English and French manuals were distributed and 2,174 individuals received instruction in Canadian Legion classes alone, not taking into account the classes operated by the other auxiliary services. I am sorry I have not the figures for the other auxiliary services, but I wish to point out that the Y.M.C.A. carries out handicraft and art classes at those stations where they operate as an auxiliary service. They are large.
To satisfy the increasing demand from service personnel for university classes the armed forces requested the Canadian Legion Educational Services to bring a full variety of courses to the attention of interested students. Bulletins which provide information relative to both English and French speaking universities have been prepared and are available to service personnel.
The three services have been giving consideration to pre-discharge training which will aid individuals in their civilian reestablishment, and at the same time provide constructive guidance during the period prior to
(Mr. LaFleche.]
demobilization. In cooperation with service representatives and representatives of the Department of Pensions and National Health, Canadian Legion educational services have provided vocational guidance manuals on some fifty gainful occupations, in addition to more comprehensive courses on the basic industries, namely, agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry.
To implement the whole educational programme requested by these sendees, Canadian Legion Educational Services have built up a large library service in Canada, Newfoundland and overseas with the following purposes in mind. I am told there are something like three hundred different textbooks. The purposes in mind are: (a) to supply prescribed and collateral readings in support of correspondence courses; (b) to provide reference texts on subjects in which oral classes have been arranged at the request of the services;
(c)	to assist the personnel to pursue studies in subjects for which correspondence courses have not as yet been provided; (d) to supply certain technical books specially useful for men in the navy, army and air force from lists approved by officers of the three branches of the service.
Reference books, both English and French, in 1942 and 1943 in Canada and Newfoundland total 71,324, being both cloth and paper bound and averaging in price about S2.50 each. Trades journals are sent out monthly to the camps in order to keep men in touch with their civil occupations, and such trade journals are provided without cost by the respective publishers.
There is a short university course for R.A.F. personnel at Bishop's university. As a result of the examples set by British universities in providing short university courses for Canadian personnel overseas, the western Quebec regional committee of the Canadian Legion sponsored a series of one-week courses at Bishop's university, Lennoxville. They were designed to provide air personnel from the Atlantic transport command particularly with information concerning Canadian affairs, and lectures and tours were provided.
So far I have been outlining the operations carried out by the Canadian Legion Educational Services in Canada and Newfoundland. May I now say something about what is being done overseas? The requirements overseas closely parallel the work performed in Canada, and is under the direction of a committee of outstanding British educationalists, the chairman of which is Sir Frederick Clarke. On this committee are also the directors of education of the three services, in addition to the Canadian Legion Educational Services overseas directors. Up to December 1943 some

TFar Appropriation-War Services
33,739 service personnel have registered for correspondence courses, and 25,407 directed reading requests were attended to.
In one month 3,106 classes were conducted with an approximate attendance of 71,059. The same text booklet or booklets and library facilities are available to Canadian personnel overseas and in any theatre of war in which our personnel serves. For instance, I am very happy to say classes were actually conducted during operations in Sicily and are being provided for at the present time in Italy.
We also do whatever we can for prisoners of war. All Canadian Legion Educational Services courses, all Canadian university courses, and whatever special courses and educational material are requested by next-of-kin, are available to Canadian prisoners of war in Germany and enemy occupied territory. Arrangements have been made through the International Red Cross Society in Geneva and the Canadian Red Cross Society to distribute such material. Examinations for all these courses are forwarded to the university of London, England, for marking, and the credits granted by that university are accepted by departments of education and universities in Canada and Newfoundland. To date some 37,787 text booklets and 662 University texts, together with 400 Canadian university correspondence courses, have been dispatched to Geneva. Some 35,981 text booklets, and library books for special reference numbering 527, have been sent to individual prisoners of war upon direct request. Some indication of the interest and value may be gained from the fact that of a total of 4,686 men in one German prisoners of war camp in October, 1943, some 2,373 attended school classes. Proof of receipt of material and appreciation of the services are received from time to time in cards and letters from the recipients and from senior Canadian and R.A.F. officers.
Now I come to the committee on education. The whole programme is supervised and co-ordinated by the national committee on education of the Canadian Legion war sei'vices, in conjunction with its regional committees in Canada, Newfoundland and overseas, under the chairmanship of Lieutenant-Colonel the Honourable Wilfrid Bovey, this committee is composed of representatives of the Canadian association of adult education, the Canadian and Newfoundland educational association, the Department of Pensions and National Health, the directors of education of the three armed services, together with two representatives of the Canadian Legion. The value of voluntary services provided by numerous outstanding men and women in Canadian and British educational fields cannot 100-144
be estimated in monetary terms. These public-spirited citizens, Mr. Chairman, I believe deserve the gratitude of all.
I have here a list of text booklets, totalling 67. I shall not venture to read them into the record, but this list is available-

Hon. members might be interested in the size of the staff required, and I have the figures as of March 31, 1944. At that time there were engaged in administrative work at headquarters 48 full-time employees. Civilian assistants, regional secretaries, clerks and stenographers, librarians and so on in the field, also full-time employees, numbered 88. Engaged in the correction of correspondence course papers were 60 part-time employees. Service personnel instructing in the field numbered 246. The number of those serving voluntarily on the national committees, the regional committees, as honorary librarians,

22S8

War Appropriation-War Services
lecturers, teachers, film specialists, operators, translators, authors and artists is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of 350. Therefore as of that date we had approximately 136 full-time employees and 906 others, both service and civilian, full-time and part-time, including those who gave their services without charge.
In regard to operations and analysis as to costs, the basis for any comparison as to increase or otherwise, at present the operations show an increase over those indicated in the six months' period ending December 31, 1943. The present ratio of expenses for headquarters administration to expenses relative to teaching is indicated by analysis of the expenditure for the six months' period ending December 31, 1943. During the period July 1, 1943, to the end of that calendar year, a total expenditure of $372,257.04 was required for the provision of educational services in Canada. Of this amount the sum of $30,169.38 was spent on headquarters administration salaries, or a percentage ratio of 8.1. The total cost of headquarters administration, including travel, rentals, furnishings and equipment, was only $37,447.22, or ten per cent of the total expenditure. The amount devoted to the provision of actual educational training and required materials, together with local regional administration, was in the sum of $311,165.93, or 83.6 per cent of the gross expenditure for the period. The balance of $23,643.89 was expended on special projects such as material for prisoners of war, preparation of material for pre-discharge training, and short courses, and represents 6.4 per cent of the total expenditure. From the above analysis it will be seen that a very modest ratio of administrative expenses obtains, and that the expenditures for actual educational purposes required the volume of the total budget. Moreover, the amount of voluntary technical, academic and advisory assistance provided by unselfish, public spirited educationists throughout Canada and Newfoundland, and I might add Great Britain, makes the total operation a most economical as well as a most efficient enterprise.
I have figures as to cost. Expenditures in Canada from the inception in October, 1939, to December 31, 1943, total $1,267,021.74. Expenditures overseas for the same period total $637,677.04.

Do I understand that the total expenditure since the war broke out is less than $3,000,000?
Mr. LaFLECHE: It is just under $2,000,000, both for overseas and in Canada.

Could the minister tell me the total budget for the services both in Canada and abroad for the current year?
Mr. LaFLECHE: You mean the year ending March 31, 1944?

Whenever the current fiscal year ends.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I must deal in fiscal
years, whereas of course the educational year ends roughly in June; we have had some little difficulty in that regard. The figures requested are, for Canada and Newfoundland, $922,000 for the year, and overseas $240,000.

Does the $922,000 include
overseas?
Mr. LaFLECHE: No, I have given them separately. Those would total $1,162,000. It is apparent that in this respect we are on the increase, and it would seem that that is only natural. Experiences of the past have permitted those carrying out these operations to perfect their systems. It has also become a matter of intimate knowledge of all members of our forces that these services are at their disposal. And they-as we, I presume-hope that this war will end in the not too distant future. It is encouraging to note that the members of our armed forces take education seriously.

For the amount of money expended, we have been told a remarkable story. I am wondering if sufficient money has been expended to make this the kind of service it ought to be. When we hear of $1,100,000 as the total expenditure for the kind of services the minister has outlined for the armed services in Canada and overseas, and for prisoners of war-and I regard that as a very important service-we must realize that relatively it is a very small sum. I am thinking of a' city of perhaps 50,000 or 60,000 inhabitants where the expenditures for public and high schools-and we might include the separate schools, too-would approach this figure. I do not know how the amount of service can be given for the money the minister has mentioned. I believe the committee would be warranted in urging that the minister discuss this matter with the national committee, to see if they are obtaining adequate sums for this important auxiliary service. I know of no service more important than the one we are now discussing.
We must remember that in this time of war we have taken from their normal way of life hundreds of thousands of young men and women who might otherwise have been completing their education. We owe it to those

War Appropriation-War Services
young people to see that the very best possible educational facilities are provided for them while they are in the armed forces. I feel this way about it, too, that if our democracy is to survive, those younger people who are serving in the armed forces and others who are growing up must be given every opportunity to appraise policies, to understand the public, social and economic environments in which we live, and be able to use democracy as it ought to be used. For, after all, in my opinion we have never had democracy. True, it was defined as government of the people, for the people and by the people; but in most of the spheres of life in which people have to move they find they are governed by selfconstituted and autocratic controllers who are anything but democratic, and who do not allow the people to exercise any degree of democracy.
My real thought is that those of us who are interested in this matter should express our appreciation of the tremendous voluntary effort undertaken, and the manner in which it has been worked out by Colonel Bovey and by the Canadian Legion. I dp not think a finer piece of work has been undertaken than the educational service for the armed forces. But in my view it has not gone far enough. 1 believe we could have spent many times the amount we have spent in this field.
I rise this afternoon, as a former teacher and one interested in education, to urge upon the committee that they see to it that this great service is in no way starved, but on the contrary is extended, fostered and financed to the very best of our ability.
I was going to ask the minister one or two questions. Is any supervision given to the amount of money asked for by the legion? Is the government advised or is the legion advised, by any committee other than those about which we have heard this afternoon? To be precise, is there a citizens' advisory committee which has any say as to the allocation of expenditures?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Perhaps I might be permitted to give a somewhat lengthy reply. It would seem to me that at this point I should explain to the committee just how all this originates, and the various steps through which proposals pass. In educational services, as in the establishment of canteens or anything else for the comfort of our fighting personnel, the requisitions arise in the defence department concerned. It may be the navy, the army or the air force. Each of the defence departments has a director of education, and it is he who says that such-and-such facilities shall be made available, and that so many people will probably wish to attend classes in 100-1441
this or that camp. That comes to my department as a proposition initiated by the defence department involved, and carrying the approval of that department. In effect it is a demand upon me to see that certain things are carried out.
While I am now speaking about educational services, the same would apply to the establishment of a hostel, a canteen, or any other service for the troops. The requisition then goes to the national war services fund advisory board, a committee composed very largely of sound, careful business men-and, of course, some women.

I should like to say a word about the national war services funds advisory board and pay a tribute to the ladies and gentlemen who serve on that board. I have appreciated their recommendations. The Minister of National War Services is not bound to accept their recommendations, but as in all cases they would have gone to the trouble of considering the merits of the proposal in detail the information they obtain is certainly worthy of the most serious consideration.

I started work at fourteen years. I think that is the best age for many children to commence work. If they are in earnest about going back to school later, most of them nowadays can find a way to do it.
In my work in the Big Brother Movement and as chairman of the Industrial School Advisory Board, I have often found it true that many boys would be better off, after fourteep years of age, to be at work than in school. Probably the fact that many boys and girls over fourteen years of age have for many years been denied the opportunity to get into work when they desired to do so has been much to the disadvantage of the social fabric of the country. Too few recognize the strain involved in the fact that most families in Canada are trying to live on a $2,000 basis with a $1,500 income.
In other words, if you put the children to work earlier, the parents can get something out of them to help meet the family budget.
A large increase in juvenile delinquency has resulted. This will not be cured by theorists, by psychologists, by social welfare workers nor by education, experts if the economic strain is forgotten. A great deal of the strain would be saved if children were allowed to take full-time jobs at fourteen years of age and then encouraged later to continue studying either at school or on their own volition.
I have read that because I have received from boys who are taking some of these courses indications that there have been delays in getting the courses, the papers and so forth, and delay's in getting the results. From the figures placed before us this afternoon I believe that that is due to an, insufficiency of facilities, too small a staff, inadequate funds, too much perhaps of voluntary work, although we all appreciate what has been done in that way; nevertheless a person who undertakes a job voluntarily very' often finds other things intervening from time to time which are his livelihood and must come first, and in that way delays may occur. I would point this out to the committee, that we are appropriating only one million dollars for this tremendously important service to which other countries are contributing as much as twenty per cent, not of their total war expenditures, but of their total expenditures on auxiliary services. By comparison our one million dollars, or one five-thousandth of the amount of money we are spending for the war, is an exceedingly small amount for this great educational service. I think that the people who are directing this service, or are responsible in any way or have any say as to the appropriation and the amount of service that shall be given ought to be people who believe in education, who do not believe, as this gentleman does, that a child of fourteen ought to be turned on to the labour market. In every progressive country in the world to-day an attempt is being made to prolong the full-time school age to
sixteen. The age of fiften has already' been adopted by many countries, and sixteen is the objective.
I think we should be careful not to allow any of our educational services to be interfered with by people who do not believe in education beyond the age of fourteen, and this gentleman evidently does not. I recognize the fact that he is a great business man and may be doing an excellent job in some other respects in connection with the auxiliary services, but I question whether anyone holding his views on education ought to be in a position where he can in any way interfere with the expenditures, which of course mean either expansion or curtailment of educational facilities. I urge upon the minister and the house that they see to it that we spend much more than we are now spending on our educational services for the army, the navy and the air force and for prisoners of war. I hope that too'will go for the entire country.
I was reading only to-day the bulletins which no doubt other members have received because evidently they are sent out from Washington on a list obtained from parliament. They are published by the Soviet Union; and I have noted over the past four or five months the tremendous expansion they are undertaking in their educational facilities, even during the war. Twenty per cent of their budget for civil projects this year is for the expansion of education in Russia. We have to keep on our toes if we are to build up the kind of Canada that most of us hope to see. We may differ as to the methods, but I believe every member of the house wants to see a better Canada than we have at the present time. I think we will all agree, no matter what our views may be as to methods, that a better Canada must be based on a sound and progressive educational policy.

there was criticism about Dieppe and Dunkirk, there was military criticism which suggested that there had been some tip-offs. But the army is followed around, in this Hollywood fashion, wherever it goes, by many organizations, all of which do good work.
The same applies in connection with these auxiliary services. Some of them are operating in connection with churches and other charitable organizations. Some organizations may want to supply a movable canteen, or to send one overseas. Under present circumstances that is not permitted, because of provisions in the War Charities Act. Well, if we are going to have a War Charities Act, then let us have a War Charities Act, or wipe it off the books altogether.
So far as I can see, the auditor general has no control over this fund. My hon. friend, the Minister of National Defence for the Army is not at the moment in his seat. However, the other night, speaking about the war expenditures committee, he said that the auditor general had control of those expenditures, and quoted from a blue book. I hold in my hand a letter from the auditor general, and I shall send a copy of it to the minister; in fact, I did send him a copy. This letter is addressed to me under date of October 2, 1942, and in it the auditor general states that everything I said was absolutely correct, and that he has no control over the war expenditures committee, nor has he any control over expenditures under the war appropriation measure.
A new officer known as the comptroller of the treasury is now in charge of any expenditures coming within the five corners of the war appropriation measure. I refer to security and defence, peace and order, the conduct of military affairs, protection of trade and the carrying out of measures deemed necessary, by order in council.
I can see very little public control over these organizations. I have before me a note with respect to sporting goods used by the auxiliary services, and that brings to mind the fact that in a pamphlet sent out from week to week by the Department of Munitions and Supply there was an item-I believe it was in the issue for last May-stating that that department had contributed 3175,000 a year to send sporting goods to the armed forces within Canada and overseas. Many organizations are doing the same thing.
I have looked into this matter as well as any hon. member, and I am convinced there is duplication by application to other departments for funds, and that some restraint should be imposed. What was the purpose of the War Charities Act? It was to protect an invasion by auxiliary organizations of the time allotted to victory loan campaigns. The public 100-145J
are asking that something be done, and that some brake or check be imposed on some of these expenditures.
Let me add that I receive many letters from the forces. I believe the minister should carry out the object of the War Charities Act, and should not allow these organizations to come here without hindrance and increase their vote from 37,000,000 to 312,000,000 in one year. There is no doubt the work done is good work, but from what I have seen of it I am convinced that there is much duplication, as there was in the last war. People club together to collect money to send equipment to the soldiers. Even the school children have been raising funds for movable motor canteens, and I say it was never intended that under the War Charities Act that this condition should exist. It was for that very purpose that, when war broke out, there was a determination not to have charity as we had it in the last war.
We are going to protect the victory loan, and see that something is done to eliminate some of the mistakes made during the last war. I know the minister has given a great deal of time to this work, because I have seen him on many occasions in Toronto. His work has been laborious, but I would ask him to try to straighten this matter out. I really believe there should be some further meeting in Ottawa of these public bodies with a view to reducing expenditures, and thereby protecting the pockets of the taxpayers. I say that because with victory loans, Red Cross campaigns, and other campaigns almost every month, I do not see where the money is to come from in this fifth year of the war.

As one listened to the statement by the minister this afternoon he could not help appreciating the great debt of gratitude owed by the citizens of Canada to the executive of the Canadian Legion. It has been through their efforts that the present educational programme has been carried on and made available to the armed services. Those people above all others in this country are deserving of the gratitude of every Canadian citizen, not only the soldiers and their relatives but those of us who live from coast to coast.
I well remember in the early days of the war suggesting to the then war services minister, the Hon. Mr. Thorson, that instead of having tag days and collections of different kinds for war charities and auxiliaries, they should be taken care of by means of taxation and a pro rata distribution made. I should like to know upon what basis distribution is made to the various organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the Salvation Army and other auxiliary services. I understand that the

War Appropriation-War Services
Red Cross is the only organization allowed to make a canvass but they must first obtain a permit from the department. I desire to know what control the minister's department has over the Red Cross in other respects.
I wish to repeat what has been said by other hon. members this afternoon and suggest that certificates of educational qualification be granted to those chaps in the armed services who are taking courses. Educational standards will mean a great deal to those chaps in the post-war period, and certificates of standing will be valuable to-them in getting employment in certain quarters.
I had an experience over the week-end when I met a young chap who had been in the Dieppe raid and was taken prisoner. He had been in a prison camp in Germany until October when he was repatriated. I was glad to learn from him that those men are now able to attend educational classes in that large prison camp. That is a worth-while project and I am glad to know that those men have an opportunity to improve their education. This chap enlisted at the outbreak of war in the Cameron Highlanders of Winnipeg. I was interested personally because he is a pal of another chap who worked on my farm prior to the outbreak of war. This man had had to work very hard all his life. He was married and had four children when he enlisted and went overseas, and I am glad to think he is now able to attend one of these classes and improve his educational qualifications.
All this is due to the Canadian Legion and its executive, and they deserve great praise for the manner in which they have carried out this work. I know that in the early stages of the war they did have difficulty in having their budgets passed by this board headed by Mr. Burton and I am glad to hear the minister say that they are now receiving practically all they ask for. I should like to have him explain how the division is made among the various auxiliary services such as the Legion, the Salvation Army and others.
We cannot say too much in praise of the volunteer efforts which have been put forth by the citizens of this country in connection with the Red Cross: Had it not been for the Red Cross many men who have been taken prisoners of war would have had a rather tough time at certain periods. The Red Cross parcels have proved a wonderful help, and we owe thanks to those citizens who have given so generously of their time and money to foster the work of this organization. Many of us do not know just how much these parcels mean to prisoners of war.
|Mr. J. A. Ross.]
Mr. LaFLECHE: The hon. member for Souris has asked about the Canadian Red Cross. Of its own volition that organization chose not to come in with the other auxiliary services. They pointed out, and have pointed out since, that the Canadian Red Cross Society is in close affiliation with the International Red Cross Society and their work is covered by conventions. Therefore they felt that they could do better work and their position would be clearer if they continued to ask Canadians to provide privately for their many requirements. As in the case of the auxiliary services, the Department of National War Services looks over the budget of the Red Cross and discusses it with them. Finally a certificate is issued to permit them to go out to try to raise so much money. It goes without saying that every hon. member and every Canadian wish the Canadian Red Cross well. They do a splendid work. A great deal of the money they obtain is used to provide food parcels for prisoners of war, not only Canadian and British but of allied countries.
I should like to say to the hon. member for Souris what I said to the hon. member for Davenport, that students who come under the Canadian Legion Educational Services will receive certificates of attainment setting out the success they have had under that plan. The hon. member wanted to know how much money was supplied to the different organizations. I can give him the figures for
1943.	While they are not up to date they will show substantially just what has taken place.
Before I give the figures I should like to reiterate that it is the Department of National Defence which says to us, "\Ve need this at such and such a place," be it a hostel, a canteen or an educational service; they tell us what is required and what auxiliary service they want to carry it out. In other words, the particular department of national defence say what they want and by whom they wish it carried out. My department does not say which auxiliary service will run the canteen at point A, the educational service at point B, the hostel at point C, or anything like that. The approximate figures for 1943 are as follows:
Canadian Legion	 $3,286,000
Knights of Columbus	 1.782,000
Salvation Army	 1,928.000
Y.M.C.A	 4.000.000
Y.W.C.A	 520.000
Navy League	 361,000
The total is approximately SI 1,900,000. The Y.W.C.A. is the only auxiliary service looking after the women of our armed forces, and it

War Appropriation-li ar Services
operates in Canada only. The Navy League operates in Canada only in so far as these figures are concerned. I would point out to the hon. member for Broadview that the auxiliary services I have just mentioned provide in Canada, in Newfoundland and overseas, the type of service for the Canadian armed services which is provided for the United States forces by the U.S.O. The American Red Cross provides the same services abroad for the United States as is provided in Canada by these auxiliary services. The navy, army and air force institute provides auxiliary services to the imperial forces similar to those provided by the organizations I have mentioned. It will be seen that it is a necessity to look after the morale and the education of the, members of the armed forces, and so far as Canadians are concerned, those necessities are made available through these organizations.
There has been an increase, and I am very happy that my hon. friend the member for Broadview brought it up. The increase is due to the very large increase there has been in the number of armed personnel as compared with the year previous. There has been an increase of over fifty per cent in the number looked after by these auxiliary services. I should like the hon. member for Broadview to believe me when I say I am satisfied there is no duplication, and that is borne out by the fact that there is one authority for these six organizations and no two operate the same service.
It will please the hon. member for Broadview who, along with others, to my knowledge has for so long been such a great worker for the returned men-I know and have always admired his very great patriotism-to learn that by reasons of the precautions taken and the arrangements made well in advance by the representatives of the auxiliary services, comforts for the soldiers went to Sicily and to Italy on the very same boats as the soldiers themselves. It is a peculiar story, but some of these comforts, cigarettes and so forth, were packed in Canadian tanks for the voyage across the water. The tanks, of course, were emptied of the comforts before they went ashore and the comforts were carried ashore separately. Therefore the representatives of these auxiliary services shared in the great glory of carrying on side by side in Sicily and Italy with our Canadian fighting men.

On July 13 of last year, at page 4751 of Hansard, the minister gave a break-down for these six or seven services, showing the estimates of their requirements and the allotments.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The figures I then gave were of expenditures. It is not possible with any degree of accuracy to estimate far in advance just what the forthcoming year will bring in the way of expenditure, because there are always changes, new institutions and new establishments. It depends to some extent upon the changes in training. The training is now pretty nearly completed, and our moving armies must be followed by these auxiliary services. That costs money, of course. The increase is due to the establishment of numerous new bases, camps and sites in Canada on both Atlantic and Pacific coasts; new services to navy personnel due to the establishment of new bases; the increase of women personnel in the forces, requiring new services, particularly the establishment of urban health centres; changes in the nature of overseas operations, including new theatres of war. The educational services were budgeted for a year and a half ago, necessarily, so that we can look after the beginning of the coming school year. Then there was the necessity for capital expenditures for the purpose of furnishing Canadian supplies in Newfoundland and in actual theatres of war. There was also an increase in navy, army and air force personnel of approximately fifty-four per cent over the previous year.

I understood that under the War Charities Act the minister was required to lay before parliament, within fifteen days after the opening of the session, a statement of the disbursement of these moneys, audited by the auditor general. Has that practice been followed?
Mr. LaFLECHE: That comes in the auditor general's report.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to add my meed of praise for the very fine work that the Canadian Legion war services is doing in bringing educational services to the young men and young women in our armed forces who desire to make use of them. Education in its broad sense is the great leavening force which, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested, will in the long run make democracy work. I do not think, however, that the word education should be narrowed down-I do not think he intended to do so-to merely scholastic training. In its broad programme the war services organization has done and is doing excellent work among our young men and our young women in the armed forces, particularly on those occasions when they might feel life becoming monotonous and when their youthful energy demands some form of activity to occupy themselves. If we can on such . occasions divert their attention to improving

War Appropriation-War Services
their minds and equipping themselves a little better to take their part in the post-war world, they themselves-and Canada-will reap a very great reward from this educational work that is being carried on under this department of government.
I do not know Mr. Burton, to whom the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has referred, but I do say that he and the members of his committee must be given some credit at least for the very fine results which the minister has laid before us this afternoon. I will go farther. Certainly I would not condemn Mr. Burton for suggesting that it might be wise for young students at the age of fourteen, or fifteen or sixteen, to go out into life.
He said fourteen.

Many educationalists of the highest repute believe that it would be a very wise thing if every student who intended to pursue higher education were given an opportunity at some stage to go out into the world and learn something of the practical things in life, learn some of those things which a good student must know if he is to make the best use of higher education.
Fourteen is normally too young for that.

I am inclined to the
opinion that fourteen may be too young, but nevertheless Mr. Burton was only suggesting their going out into the world for a period and from my experience in my own family I consider it a wise thing to do, so that the young student, having gained actual experience in the practical things of life, will then take up his education with a new purpose and a new energy to equip himself for life. Undoubtedly he will be benefited greatly by that period of settling down, shall I say, into a purpose that will guide him in the avocation he has chosen. It happened to be my privilege to meet some of the officials in charge of this particular work, and cerainly nothing that I learned on that visit to the headquarters of the Canadian war services lessened the admiration which I have for the work that is being done.
I was told of one incident which will illustrate the real value of education as a morale builder, apart from the training which is given by any educational programme. I believe that many persons, particularly young people, have a sense of inferiority which may develop into a complex if, in this day and age, they find themselves not equipped with reasonable educational qualifications. I was informed that out of a number of army units-regiments or battalions-about one hundred indivdiuals were about to be discharged as unlikely to become efficient soldiers. Anybody who has been

in the army knows that in any battalion there are certain individuals who do not fit in and cannot apparently become an efficient part of army life. Consequently these men were being drained out of these battalions and were about to be discharged, when it was suggested that they be brought together and that some examination be made of the factors which rendered them unfit for the duty which was being asked of them. The result of the experiment was remarkable. These men were discovered to be quite illiterate. They could not write and they could not read. Not knowing what was posted on the order board, or able to read any publications, they were incapable of participating in the discussion and appreciation of the orders and documents which were being distributed among their comrades. Accordingly the Canadian Legion war services undertook the task of teaching them to read and write. I shall not enlarge on what was done, but I would point out the result. Of the hundred individuals involved in this experiment, eighty were returned to their battalions, and their subsequent records were those of fine, able members of our Canadian army forces.
That is an extreme instance of the value of education. It shows that the real reason why these young men did not fit into army life was their complete inability to appreciate the nature and purposes of the tasks imposed upon them. To them these tasks seemed nothing but drudgery, a series of regulations and orders which perhaps irritated them and aroused their antagonism. The ability to read and write gave them an opportunity to appreciate the contribution they were making, so that they went back to their units with an entirely different viewpoint. Of course, in all walks of life, including our own, and at all ages, further education along proper lines greatly increases morale and heightens the appreciation we have of the part we play in life.
For this reason, while I do not know that the department over which the minister presides is not sufficiently generous toward this particular project, I urge upon the minister the advisability of making generous provision to carry on this very fine work.
One thought which gave me some concern as I gave consideration to the work of this particular branch in connection with our armed services was that the young men and women who perhaps least of all need this assistance are the most likely voluntarily to take advantage of it and to devote the time and effort necessary to equip themselves, and unfortunately those who most need this assistance will be the last to volunteer. I suggest to the minister that he strongly urge those in charge of this particular programme to see to it, not only that the opportunity is given to all

New Brunswick Railway Company
these young men and young women, but that a certain amount of encouragement-not compulsion-is given to those who most need it to take advantage of the opportunities of training in some particular line. You can lead a horse to water but you cannot make it drink. Sometimes, however, by wise methods you can persuade it. I suggest to the minister that that is one point to keep in mind, namely, that most likely those who readily volunteer to take advantage of this splendid opportunity will be those who least need it, and an effort should be made to bring to the attention of those who do not appreciate it, the advantages to be gained in equipping themselves for later life.
We have learned with great interest of the programme of post-war rehabilitation. This is an important opportunity which, if made use of, will prepare those who take advantage of it, either not to require government assistance in rehabilitating themselves, or, if they do require it, the better to take advantage of it.
In conclusion, I would1, as I say, add my meed of praise to the organization itself and to the committee of volunteers who have made possible the results which the minister has outlined to-day. It is a great work, and we can readily and wisely provide the funds which will enlarge and expand and make even greater and finer the results already achieved.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. H. R. EMMERSON (Westmorland) moved the second reading of bill No. 39, respecting the New Brunswick Railway Company.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: So far as I can recall I do not think that on the introduction of this bill or on the first reading of it the hon. member who is introducing it gave any comprehensive statement as to its effect. This would seem to be the appropriate time to have that done.

Mr. Speaker, this bill had its origin in the senate and was passed by the senate on March 22 of this year. The purpose of this bill is to enable the company to reduce its capital by paying off pro rata among its shareholders paid-up capital which is now in excess of its wants. .
The company was incorporated in 1870 by chapter 49 of the statutes of New Brunswick. In 1881 the work of the company was declared to be work for the general advantage of Canada, and the company is subject to the jurisdiction of parliament and to the Railway Act. On July 1, 1890, the company leased and demised all its lines of railroad, having an aggregate length of about 420 miles, and all the company's plant, rolling stock and equipment, to the Caandian Pacific Railway Company for a term of 990 years. As a matter of fact, the railway has become part and parcel of the Canadian Pacific railway system in New Brunswick.
By this lease, subsequently made binding on both parties by parliament in 1891, the Canadian Pacific Railway company undertook to maintain and operate the railway system and the New Brunswick Railway company agreed to maintain the corporate existence of the company until the termination of the lease. It is accordingly impossible for the company to go into voluntary liquidation and distribute its assets. Apart from the railway properties the only remaining assets of the company were certain freehold timber lands in New Brunswick which had been granted to it by way of subsidy when the original lines were constructed.
Since 1890 the business of the company has consisted solely in managing these timber lands, granting stumpage rights, and from time to time selling portions of them. In recent years these lands have consisted of about 1,600,000 acres; a substantial portion of this acreage has now been sold to purchasers in New Brunswick, and the purchase prices have already been paid or shortly will be paid in full. The result is that the company will have on hand capital in excess of its requirements. The capital stock of the company consists of 30,000 fully paid shares of the par value of $100 each.
Under the Dominion Companies Act a company incorporated by letters patent can reduce its capital and pay off any paid-up capital which is in excess of its wants (section 49).
Under the Railway Act power is given to a company to increase its capital stock from time to time, subject to the approval of two-thirds of the shareholders and of the governor in council (section 78), but no general provision is made for reduction of capital. Consequently in each case it is necessary to apply to parliament for legislation permitting such reduction.

New Brunswick Railway Company
In the present bill the by-law enacting the reduction has to be confirmed by at least two-thirds of the shareholders and subsequently by the governor in council, after publication of notices of the application for the reduction. In practice this would mean that the governor in council would act on a report and recommendation of the Minister of Transport, because the New Brunswick Railway Company falls within the jurisdiction of his department. The company would, naturally, satisfy the Minister of Transport that they had taken care of liabilities and had funds on hand with which to pay off their shareholders.
I understand that the Minister of Transport has no objection to the bill nor has the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is also my understanding that the income tax authorities have no objection to this bill which, in point of fact, merely gives the company, which is to all intents and purposes a land company, the same rights as any other company subject to section 49 of the Dominion Companies Act.
Full details and explanations will be given by those representing the company when the bill comes before the railway committee.
Could the hon. member tell us why this bill came in the back door of the Senate instead of coming into the House of Commons?
I understand that is usual. I know of no reason why it came in the back door as the hon. member suggests.
That is what makes me suspicious. I wonder why that was done.
Private bills are usually introduced in the first instance in the senate, which explains why this reference comes from the other house to this house.
Why the exception in the case of bill No. 37?
What is the amount involved in this bill?

I am afraid I cannot give the details of that, but that information can be supplied when the bill is in committee. The capitalization of the company is 30,000 fully paid-up shares at $100 each. I make that $3,000,000.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

The following news item appeared in the Ottawa Evening Journal of February 17, 1944:
Four Canadian women-Mrs. Gordon Konantz of Winnipeg, Miss Agathe Dore of Montreal, Mrs. Jules Laine of Toronto and Miss Helen Doherty of Ottawa-have arrived in the United Kingdom to study the voluntary war work of British women's organizations, the war services department announced Wednesday. The trip was sponsored by the department.
Different fields of study have been allotted to each of the party, so that as w'ide a survey as possible could be made in the time available. The visit wall include both rural and urban centres in the United Kingdom.
The four reports to the department will deal not only with women's war activities but also with their plans for work in the post-war period.
Another item appearing in the same newspaper under date of January 4, 1944, reads:
While the war services department refused to give any information, Liberal ward workers in Ottawa West to-day were protesting the appointment of Miss Helen Doherty to head a delegation of four women on an "inspection" trip to Britain.
Miss Doherty, former secretary of the National Liberal Federation of Women, and now special assistant to War Services Minister LaFleehe, has been assigned to survey the work done -in Britain by women's volunteer organizations.
And further:
It had been established by this morning that the Catholic Women's League, the Red Cross, Protestant Women's organizations, the Y.W.C.A. and other organizations, which have been doing the actual work in voluntary services, had not been consulted on the appointments.
Miss Doherty left her post in 1940 as secretary of the national federation of Libera] women and shortly afterwards received an appointment to the war services department.
On March 18, 1943, I asked certain questions in regard to Miss Doherty, as follows:
1.	In what capacity is Miss Helen Doherty employed in the Department of National War Services?
2.	What are the duties attached to such position?

War Appropriation-War Services
3.	How long has she been employed in such position?
4.	What is the total remuneration which has been paid to 'her, either by way of salary or honorarium?
5.	What is the total which has been paid to her by way of travelling expenses and living allowance?
The minister gave the following information:
1.	General assistant.
2.	Assists generally, makes surveys and special studies of activities of the department, exercises supervision as required.
3.	Two years and six months.
4.	$9,190.

The minister stated that this lady made surveys for the department. Later on I should like him to tell us what surveys she has made. Then on March 24, 1943, I asked another question:
What sums and on what dates were payments made to Miss Helen Doherty as special assistant to the Minister of National War Services?
