On March 5, 1941, the hon. member for Huron North asked these questions:
1.	Is Miss Helen Doherty employed in the Department of National War Services?
2.	If so, in what capacity?
3.	When was she appointed?
4.	What salary or other remuneration is paid to her?
5.	Was she assigned to this position by the civil service commission?
6.	If so, on what date was the assignment made?
7.	If no assignment was made by the civil service commission, by whom was the appointment made and under what authority?
8.	Was any request made to the civil service commission for the appointment of Miss Doherty to such position?
9.	If so, what action did the civil service commission take thereon?
I should like the minister to answer thes6 questions, and I wish to ask further why it is necessary for Miss Doherty to visit this House of Commons quite frequently. I know she was around last session. I do not think she called upon any of the Progressive Conservative members or any of the members belonging to the other opposition groups, but certainly she paid visits to Liberal members and senators. I should like to know what amount Miss Doherty received by way of expenses for her trip to Britain, and what the other women received. I should like to know also if we can get a copy of any report that may have been made as a result of this trip. I think the committee would like to know what Miss Doherty does in the department, and also why the lump sum of $7,090 was paid to her. I think it is very unusual to pay a lump sum to a person who is supposed to have been in the sendee for two years. Why was she not paid on a monthly basis from the very first?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I take it, Mr. Chairman, that the questions which have been read by the hon. member have been answered in this house.

Partly answered.
Mr. LaFLECHE: As to the matter the hon. gentleman mentioned a moment ago, in regard to this young lady visiting the House of Commons, I have no knowledge of that unless it was to call at my office with reports when she had occasion to do so, as do other employees of my department. As to her expenses for the trip to Great Britain, and the expenses of the other ladies, I have no knowledge; this is the first time that question has been asked, but I shall be very happy to get the information and bring it down in the house. My hon. friend asks what Miss Doherty does. When the Department of National War Services was first contemplated a staff had to be found, a plan of organization had to be drawn up and certain positions had to be filled. I have it on good authority that at the very beginning this lady was considered for a position carrying a remuneration greater than she is now paid. I do not know precisely what was in mind but I have seen a proposed plan of organization under which the. department was to have been divided into four divisions, and Miss Doherty was under consideration to head one of these divisions at that time. That did not materialize. Yet she had been called into the department in August or September, 1940, on the understanding that she was being called in to take over the work. I think she was given an idea of about what

War Appropriation-War Services
was in mind by way of organizing the department. She remained there and, finally, at the time mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough West, she was paid at the rate of $10 a day, if I remember correctly, for the time she had put in in the department.
Then she was appointed general assistant, or special assistant, at a rate of $3,600 a year. That is the story of Miss Doherty's coming into the department and remaining there. Since then Miss Doherty has gone to Great Britain, with three other ladies, to represent the department there. She has returned, and with the other three ladies is busy writing a report of what was seen. Since her return, however, she has taken on other duties, one having to do with discussions concerning repatriates, which have just arisen, and about which I do not know very much myself.
Another piece of work she has taken on for the department-or for me, if you like- has been to follow the proceedings of the special Committee of the House of Commons on radio broadcasting. Then, again, since her return to Canada, very recently also she has been a member of an interdepartmental committee in respect of UNRRA, which was mentioned last week in the house.
That, I regret, is, as well as I can remember, the hon. member's questions.
Would the minister tell us why these four women were picked? How were they picked?

The department picked
them; you would ask.

I
know I have asked ;* we want to know.
You ought to know.
We want to know.

I should like to know
what difference there will be, so far as the interests of the general public are concerned. Every member who rises from the other side of the house-not every one, but some of them-always says, "I want to know, and the people want to know". Do the people ask you to find that out?

The people of Canada certainly need to know where their money is going. And any hon. member in this house who thinks they do not want to know is absolutely wrong. The hon. member who has just spoken has made a very peculiar statement. It is a statement which will go down with this government, and will help to put the government absolutely out of power when the next election comes

along. The hon. member who has just spoken knows perfectly well that money is being spent which should not be spent.

I have asked why this lady was appointed. I have asked by whom she was appointed. I have asked why she was appointed and who appointed her to go overseas, and how those ladies were appointed. There are women across Canada-thousands of them-doing voluntary

He is the hon. member for Carleton. I do not know why so much fuss should be made about this particular case. It was said a moment ago that I recommended this appointment. I do not like to ask my hon. friend to withdraw because it is picayune business on the part of any hon. member to speak of recommendations.

I will say "small," if you do not like the word "picayune." My English has been learned on the street.
You have a lot to learn all right.
Are you going to be my teacher?
I certainly should not like to be.
These things should not be brought up when we are doing the best we can to win the war.
Who are "we"?

The minister is endeavouring to conduct his department in the best interests of the general public and I cannot understand why we should lose so much time over such a small item. My hon. friend may like to do this, probably from a sense of fear, but I dislike it. I do not think it is proper. I do not think it can be said that this department has thrown away one five-cent piece, that it has not made all the expenditures it has made in the interests and for the advancement of the country.
Was it not Caesar who said, Methinks thou protest too much, dear Brutus?
My friend protests too much about his honesty.

I have never said I was honest, but I hope I am. The hon. gentleman has said that I only go after small things. The reason why we have to deal with small things of this kind is that when we get into the big money, the items where millions are spent or thrown away, as the hon. gentleman said himself, we cannot get an answer. If the hon. gentleman will look at page 1041 of Hansard of March 2 he will see that I asked a question with regard to shipbuilding, which means millions and millions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member realizes that we are not on shipbuilding. I hope hon. members will keep within the item that is before the committee at the moment.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I just wanted to show the hon. member that I have tried to get proper answers. Whenever that has happened we are told by the government that it is not in the public interest. I want to tell the hon. gentleman and this committee that the people of Canada are interested in where their money goes. That is why I asked the question I did to-night. I should like to get an answer. I should like to know why

these four women were picked. I should like to know who selected them to go overseas. I should like to know whether the women doing volunteer war work were consulted as to who should go. I do not think they were, but I want to know.

Perhaps I could amplify the question somewhat. The hon. member for Ottawa East seems to know a lot about Miss Helen Doherty. Probably he can tell the minister and he will be able to give us some of the answer's to these questions. What was Miss Helen Doherty doing before she went into the Department of National War Services? What was she doing during the two years for which she received $7,090? Upon whose recommendation was she appointed? What were her peculiar qualifications for the work she was doing? What was the pay of the two women who went over with her? What report did she make? We should be given full details of that report. I am sure if the minister cannot answer these questions the hon. member for Ottawa East will be able to help him since the hon. member seems to know so much about Miss Doherty. This is an item of $9,000, but if the hon. member for Ottawa East thinks that $9,000 paid to a lady for two years' services is picayune and if he knows of other occasions where money is being wasted, probably he will tell the committee and we will try to get to the bottom of them. This thing is in the fire, so let us pull it out of the embers.

The hon. member's question is so elaborate that I would ask him to put it on the order paper and I shall try to answer.
Mr. LaFLECHE: If I am permitted I shall do my best to give an answer. I trust that my words will not be taken amiss when I say that as far as I am concerned personally it is a matter of regret that the names of individuals who cannot be here to defend themselves are mentioned, as occurs at times. The question of the payment of public money is a matter of great importance; every hon. member has a right to ask his question and every question should be answered carefully and correctly. No one has a greater interest in the careful spending of money than those who have the honour to be members of the administration. As far as the department over which I have the honour to preside is concerned, 1 make bold to say that great care is taken in expending the people's money. I have been told by the civil service commission at times that I was attempting to run my department too economically. I leave that statement with the hon. members of this committee.
To return to the case in point, when the lady whose name has been mentioned this

War Appropriation-War Services
evening first joined the department there was no staff; there were no superintendents; there were no directors; this was a department that started at full speed before there was time to get it organized. All the employees of the department-they will be glad to confirm this if necessary-were going night and day for at least the first year and a half, each doing what he could to see that the work was kept up to date. Among these was the lady whose name has been mentioned this evening. The payment that was made to her was made a long time after she had carried out her work. She rendered great assistance to the department, but because of a series of events it was impossible for her to be paid. This went on from month to month and year to year with the employee not being paid and nevertheless not protesting, although that was not a very comfortable position for anybody to be in. Pinally my predecessor saw to it that it was made possible to pay the lady. The larger amount mentioned by the hon. member was such only because it covered nearly three years.
The question of sending the ladies overseas to represent the department arose early in 1943 when I, as Minister of National War Services, thought it would be helpful in promoting the contribution of all Canadian women to the dominion's war effort to send a small delegation of Canadian women representing the Department of National War Services to survey what was being done in Great Britain by the women of that country, and upon their return to report on what they had seen. Then that information would be made available to all Canadian women through their organizations or otherwise. The Dowager Marchioness of Reading, Chairman of the Women's Yoijntary Services for Civil Defence in the United Kingdom, having learned of my intention in this regard, last May indicated that her organization would be delighted to extend every possible cooperation to the ladies who would come from Canada to survey the work being done by the women of that country in Britain's war effort. At a business conference of the Canadian women's voluntary services and others in Ottawa on June 28, 29 and 30,	1943, I expressed the hope-I
announced, if you like-that the war services department would try to send a delegation of three or four Canadian women to study and report upon the operation of British women's organizations doing patriotic war work.
In this house, Mr. Chairman, in reply to a series of questions by the hon. member for Danforth on July 12, 1943, I set out precisely how the choice of the department's representatives would be made, and that procedure was followed. My proposal, as I thought was thus made clear from the very outset, contemplated a somewhat broader mission than merely sending representatives who would confine their activities to surveying any one women's organization in the United Kingdom, and was designed to make available to all Canadian women information that they could use to the best advantage in their work in Canada. It must be remembered that there are many women's organizations doing patriotic work in Canada, just as there are in the United Kingdom, and the, Department of National War Services has a broad and continuing responsibility to assist, in whatever way may be possible, the Canadian women doing patriotic work in Canada in support of the war effort.
No objection reached me following my statement in this house on July 12, 1943, in reply to a series of questions by the hon. member for Danforth as to how the department's delegation would be chosen, and I proceeded accordingly as had been announced.
The members of the department's delegation were Mrs. Gordon Konantz of Winnipeg, Miss Dore of Montreal, Mrs. Laine of Toronto and from the department, largely for departmental purposes, Miss Helen Doherty of Ottawa. Since Mrs. Konantz and Miss Dore were prominently identified with women's voluntary services working in Canada, quite naturally they were assigned the duty of observing what was being done by the women's voluntary services for defence in Great Britain. Mrs. Laine, who had been active and very successful in regard to other women's work, and Miss Doherty who has a splendid record of work in connection with women's work, and particularly in work for returned soldiers, were given other assignments.
I should like to emphasize that these four Canadian women were chosen, not as individuals representing any particular group, but as representatives of the department, with special emphasis in the case of two of these ladies in connection with women's voluntary service work. One departmental official was included for the obvious and necessary purpose of ensuring continuity in the interests of the department and of patriotic work by all women's organizations in the dominion. It was necessary, however, before the ladies left Canada, to deal with this matter with great secrecy for security reasons, to safeguard the delegation in travelling by boat to and from the United Kingdom in the midst of hazardous war-time conditions at sea.

Maybe because they did not apprehend all aspects of my intentions and of the department's intention in sending the departmental delegation to Great Britain to examine the patriotic work of all women's organizations there for the benefit of all Canadian women's organizations and of all Canadian women, some ladies in Canada were moved to express regret that the delegation was not composed exclusively of women identified with women's voluntary service work here. My conception of the situation and of the requirement was that if we took up any women's work we had to do our best to take up all of it, and that will be the result when we read the reports from these four ladies. I have already said this evening that the four ladies in question are now busy writing their reports.
I should like to add that the ladies in question, each one of them, were highly recommended to me. In the case of Miss Doherty, she being a departmental employee, that matter was not of so much significance as in the case of the other three. Not only were they very highly recommended, but the reports I have had from Lady Reading in Great Britain are that she had great admiration for the work these ladies did over there. I hope to have their reports soon, when they will be brought to the attention of all Canadian women's organizations for their information and, I trust, for their assistance. I think that is the answer which my hon. friend requested.

I wish the minister to understand that I have absolutely nothing against Miss Doherty or any of the other ladies. It is wholly a question of how these people are engaged and how they are paid. The minister said that it was owing to a series of events that Miss Doherty was not paid for over two years-almost three years, he said. He did not tell us what the series of events was, or why, when she was hired, no provision was made in the order in council for payment. I asked, what did Miss Doherty receive for expenses on the British trip; how long was she on that trip; did the other ladies receive their expenses; did they receive any salary, or how was the matter worked?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Miss Doherty being a departmental employee, her pay continued. All the ladies were given the same amount of expense money. I am sorry that, since I did not know the question was coming up, I have not the figures. Mrs. Laine, one of these ladies, has advised the department that she will not put in any claim. She not only offered 
her time but has declined to accept any expense money. That is greatly to be admired. It is only fair to say, however, that it is not possible for all persons under such circumstances to refund advances and to decline to put in their accounts. However fine it is, it is something we shall all agree cannot be expected of everyone.

I quite agree with the minister that there are many women who cannot afford to pay their own way, and who should be reimbursed. Perhaps at the next sitting the minister will be able to tell us what they got.
Mr. LaFLECHE: If I may, I will treat it as a question,
Yes.

The minister in discussing this last matter said that Miss Doherty had been engaged in radio broadcasting. I have had many letters from people in western Canada asking about a Miss Claire Wallace, who is engaged in radio broadcasting, and I have received many newspaper clippings, and inquiries as to what salary and what expense account this lady receives from the government. If this comes under the minister's jurisdiction I believe it would be well, in the interests of the country, if we could have a satisfactory answer immediately. Many people are asking if this woman is worth her hire in the matter of war savings stamps. I believe that is the chief reason why she is engaged; and since the sixth victory loan is just now being launched many people may make this matter an excuse for dilatoriness about subscribing to the loan. Perhaps the minister would give a detailed statement of what this lady's salary and expense account have been during, say, 1943; what salary she now receives per month, and what expenses she is allowed. It would give our fellow citizens who are trying to sell victory bonds an opportunity to clear up possible misconceptions, because this question is very interesting at the present time to many people throughout western Canada.

speechtext:

minister answers, may I say this. We are now discussing the item of war charities. I hope it will be found possible to restrict the discussion to that item.

speechtext:

War Appropriation-War Services
Mr. LaFLECHE: I trust that, when we come to other items which have already been discussed, hon. members will recall the fact.
I welcome questions such as have been put this evening. The hon. member for Souris mentioned Miss Claire Wallace. I regret very much that I am not the competent authority to answer. I have seen, of course, something in the press, and the matter was brought up in the radio committee. But the lady is not employed by my department or by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I believe she was given some work to do, that her services were required by the war finance ' committee. To give any figures would be to guess, and I hesitate to do that. But the matter is not in my department.	#

The reason why I
asked this question on administration was in order that the minister, if it related to the C.B.C., could deal with it. I now understand that she probably is hired by the war finance committee to sell war savings certificates. I do not know anything about this myself, but 1 have had dozens, if not hundreds of letters from many parts of the west in recent months, and because some people are making it an excuse to hesitate about subscribing to the victory loan, the sooner the matter can be cleared up, the better. I may have to wait to ask the Minister of Finance, but I thought it might be answered under the C.B.C. item.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I feel very much as the hon. member does, and I can only say that I regret very much that I have not the information. All I could say would be guesswork, and he does not want that.

Oh, no. It has been reported that this lady now receives $200 a week and an expense account. If the minister could get the information and give it on behalf of the government, it would be in the interests of the country to have the matter cleared up quickly.

I do not want to interrupt the continuity of discussion; that, perhaps, is one thing which frequently happens when we are in committee. From one matter we jump to another; then we return to the first subject, then jump to something else, and so on.
This afternoon the minister gave us quite an adequate picture of the courses which are administered through his department to men serving in the armed forces. I should like to know whether his department is responsible for the lectures which are now being given in various branches of the armed services with respect to post-war rehabilitation. A series of lectures is being given to inform
members of the armed forces of what will be done for them after the war. If this activity comes under the minister's department, I should like the opportunity of discussing it now. If it does not come under his department, would he tell us what department has to do with it, so that I may discuss it under the appropriate item?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I understand that the
lectures in question are prepared primarily by the directors of education of the defence departments and by the Canadian Legion's educational officers. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if the hon. member wishes to discuss an item it might be better to wait until we get to the next one; but, since we have not differentiated so far, this is just as good a time as any.

It does not matter very much really, whether it comes under the minister's department or not. The only point is I want to be in order. I think we are all aware that a series of lectures is being given to members of our armed forces on the matter of their rehabilitation when the war is over. I should like some information in that respect and perhaps the other ministers can give it to me. What sort of lectures are they and who prepares them; who are the officers who are lecturing? I understand it is an officer in the particular camp where the lectures are given who gives the lecture. Who prepares these courses? Are the officers competent to give lectures? Who informs them as to what the rehabilitation programme is to be? I have talked with quite a few men in the forces with respect to those lectures. I wonder why the lectures are given. I have no objection to the soldiers being informed as to what the country is to do for them after the war, but I wonder whether there may not be a principle involved. Is it because the members of the armed forces are getting a little restless as to what may happen to them, and we have to pacify them by telling them this?
There is another principle involved and I do not want to be misunderstood as I propound what is in my mind. In making a speech or answering a question the other day the minister said we had to have faith. My work for a good many years taught me that I had to live by faith, and perhaps I know just a little bit about that. There was a time in my life when I used to make it a rule, because I thought it was quite ethical to do so, to trust everyone and consider that everyone was honest until I found that they could not be trusted because they were not honest. I thought that was a pretty good rule to follow in those days, but I have been in politics now for a few years and it seems to me-perhaps

War Appropriation-War Services
I have fallen a little bit from those high ideals-that I am gradually unconsciously slipping into that place where I do not trust anybody, and consider that everybody is a crook until I make extremely sure he is just and honest. That seems to be about the way I have a tendency to feel. I hate myself for it. But somehow or another that is the life of one who is in politics very long.
I cannot see what kind of lecture can be given to these men on post-war rehabilitation except a lecture on what the present government proposes to do for them. I cannot see what they can be told, apart from the legislation that is at present on the statute books or the legislation that the present government is contemplating bringing down this session.
They can be told to vote Liberal.

My hon. friend says they can be told to vote Liberal. I would not go so far as to accuse any officer giving those lectures of deliberately doing that. But what is the result? What can be expected? It seems to me that it is only natural to say that if the lecturer satisfies the men in the armed forces that the government who is preparing this legislation is going to look after them when the war is over, naturally they will go away with the impression-well, I guess it is a pretty good government after all; I guess we will have to put the X mark down in the right place, and so forth. I hope I am not overemphasizing my fear in that respect, but I believe that is the natural tendency.
Of course, the only proper thing that could be done to offset that would be for officers to be trained and schooled in what all of the other parties in this country would like to do for the returned soldier. In that way the men in the forces would be able to know that between the three in some way or another they would be looked after, and then perhaps the tendency would not be as it is to-day. I believe the lectures that are given to-day on the basis of the present legislation are a bit lopsided.
There is another point. I do not know whether the minister is aware of this, but these lectures are compulsory. The members of the forces are paraded and they have to listen to them whether they want to or not. I hope I do not go to the extreme when I say there is a possibility that the members of the armed forces are forced to listen to our Liberal friends' programme. I am voicing that observation. I trust the minister as much as anyone else does. I have as much faith as anyone else has, but unfortunately I believe that to be the case.

Mr. LaFLECHE:	I do not think it is for
me to reply to the respected hon. member for Macleod in regard to faith, but I may tell him that the saddest thing is to lose one's faith, and if he would be happy to believe not only in God, but as far as he can in man, it would be a fine thing.
In regard to the lectures mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod I think I explained that they are prepared by the educational officers of national defence working with Canadian Legion educational officers. I do not know that any of those lectures are compulsory; but having been in that position myself for a long time, it may well be that some conscientious commanding officer would parade his men to hear those lectures because he believed in them himself. It is not correct, I am sure, to think, and even less to suggest that these lectures are in the nature of an appeal to vote in favour of the administration. If one were to express one's full thoughts on such a matter one might guess, perhaps, that certain zealous persons might have infiltrated behind the lines and there had some effect upon what was said; but I think in both cases one would be wrong. The motives of these people who work to educate others are good. The commanding officer is there to watch how things are going. I have not heard any stories which would substantiate in my mind the thought which has been expressed by the hon. member for Macleod. I trust that this will be accepted by the hon. member as a reply to his question, but, if not, I shall be glad to listen to and try to answer any other questions he may care to ask.

In connection with the board, headed by Mr. Burton, which was mentioned this afternoon, I endeavoured to follow the minister as closely as possible and he may have given the information I want, but, if so, it did not come to my notice. Would the minister say in what manner the members of this board were chosen. In other words, how did he go about ferreting out the individuals who compose this board? For example, did he obtain recommendations from the various organizations or associations which receive grants? Did he obtain recommendations from the Canadian Legion, the Knights of Columbus, the Navy League of Canada, the Salvation Army and so on? How were the members from the various provinces selected and appointed to this board? Then I wish the minister would tell the committee what expenses have been incurred by the board since its organization. I understand the members are not in receipt of any salary, but perhaps the minister would tell us the number of meetings that have been held, the

War Appropriation-War Services
per diem allowances, if any, which have been paid the members of the board, and the total expenses to date.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I should like to point out that these ladies and gentlemen were appointed at least two years before I became head of this department, and I am not in a position to say how they were chosen.

You were the deputy minister, were you not?
Mr, LaFLECHE: This came under my associate, the Hon. Mr. Justice T. C. Davis; it did not come under my direction at that time. I am not in a position to say how the members of the board were chosen; but from a few things I have heard I make bold to suggest to my hon. friend that he need have no fear whatsoever of any desire on their part, even three and a half years ago or whenever they were named, to play a game on the loyal opposition.

I am not suggesting anything like that; I just want to get the information.
Mr. LaFLECHE: May we look upon them as good Canadians and judge their value from that one point of view alone? If I were permitted to do the judging I would and I do assure hon. members that these people are excellent citizens; they are very hard workers; they are. conscientious. I owe them this further tribute: they seem to have taken great care to see that the Minister of National War Services is always kept in a safe position in regard to approving expenditures. That is what I would expect of ordinary departmental officials, and I feel deep gratitude to these people. Yet I find them broad-minded and personally extremely generous, though very careful with the money of the taxpayers. I like Canadians like that.

If I may interrupt with another question, I do not know anything about it but I want to find out the basis on which the representation was obtained. For example, on what basis would they go to Saskatchewan and select a man? On what basis would they go to British Columbia and select a man? Was it in reference to the type of work they had to do or the experience they possessed; was it in reference to any recommendations which might have been made, and, I think, should have been made, by the organizations interested?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have already said that I am not aware of the basis of their choice; but speaking of them as persons who are members of the board and judging them from
that point of view alone, I do give my hon. friend my assurance that there is not a poor selection in the entire membership.

Were they appointed by the Hon. Mr. Justice Davis, or were they appointed by some other person in the department?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	They were appointed
when the present Minister of Agriculture was the Minister of National War Services. His successor, now the Hon. Mr. Justice Thorson, renewed their term, and I also have renewed their term; at least on my recommendation they have been appointed for another year. As far as I recall, this is the first time this question has been raised. Just what I mean by that I do not know myself, except that as far as my knowledge goes their appointment has never been questioned, and I do not believe their actions can be questioned.
If I may continue with my answer, there are about ten meetings a year of the full committee and/or the executive committee. Members of the board receive no salary ; travelling expenses are paid, but a number of the members pay their own expenses. The cost of the meetings on a yearly basis is about $4,000. I hope that answers my hon. friend.

I am not satisfied yet. I do not wish to cast any reflection upon these gentlemen; from what the minister says I assume that they are perfectly reputable citizens. I want to find out how well they are qualified to judge the sort of things they have to judge in connection with these matters, and I thought perhaps the minister might be able to give us some lead as to why different individuals were appointed to that board; their knowledge of education, for example, or their knowledge of - returned men, or their knowledge of some particular phase of the matters wffiich they must take under consideration.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I would point out that
when these ladies and gentlemen were first appointed, the whole of Canada was being combed for persons who would consent to take on such difficult and onerous jobs. I do not know what the authorities had in mind at that time by way of necessary qualifications. There would hardly be reason for exacting, in any great number of cases, knowledge of education or educational methods, because at that time educational matters were but one subject of many that had to be dealt with. The putting up of canteens and hospitals and things like that, I imagine, were of much greater urgency than anything else. As time has gone on, however, educational matters have properly assumed greater importance, but these ladies and gentlemen who were named

War Appropriation-War Services
at that time know the work and the details of these organizations. I have seen them at work a number of times; I make it my business to attend their meetings whenever possible. They are good enough to invite me to the table; they do the talking and I do the listening. I do not interfere with their decisions, which are laid before me later, but it has seemed to me that each member of the board appeared to understand the problem thoroughly. I should say that each member of the present board is an excellent member. If he did not have the particular qualifications at the beginning I think he has acquired them by practice, as so many attainments are acquired.

As far as the minister knows, then, these men were not appointed as the result of recommendations made by the various organizations who share in the grant that is made?
Mr. LaFLECHE; I do not know, I am sorry. I have no knowledge of that.

I agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon City and with other hon. members who spoke earlier in the debate. In my view the time has passed when this remote control organization, known as the Burton committee, can serve any useful purpose. I could understand that when the Department of National War Services was first set up, because it was a new department entering a new field under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture, it was entering upon duties concerning which he had very little knowledge. He had to reorganize the whole thing, from the bottom to the top, and I could understand his desire to set up a committee similar to the Burton committee to assist in scrutinizing the expenditures.	*
I think, however, the time has come when the present minister is in charge of a pretty thoroughly organized department. The defence organizations, which recommend in the first instance, and the auxiliary services, have well-defined organizations. I cannot see how a committee comprised of people from one end of Canada to the other, and particularly of very busy people, can be of much use. We were told this afternoon that unfortunately Mr. Burton is ill, and that leaves him out of the picture at the present time. However, when he is enjoying his good health he is very busy in other fields. I am sure, too, that Mr. Wallace R. Campbell is a very busy man in Windsor at the present time, bcause he heads a large organization. I cannot see how that board, which would have the final say in respect of any recommendation coming from the army, the navy, the air force or the
[Mr. LaFleche.l
auxiliary services, in connection with any extension or expansion of service, could do anything but block, or act as something which would retard progress. It has to be called together from all parts of Canada.
For example, the Canadian Legion war services may decide that they need literature, textbooks or printing. But before they can go ahead with their educational work they must secure requisitions from the committee. A month or two may elapse between the meetings of that committee. Meantime the Legion services, or other auxiliary services, are waiting for an approval from the board.
It is my view that the time has arrived when the board is no longer necessary. With the four years' experience they have had, I believe the defence and auxiliary services are in a position to-day to conduct the affairs of their departments through the Minister of National War Services. That organization is sufficiently well developed now, under a permanent minister, to be able to say just how the money which is being appropriated by parliament is to be spent. I believe it is desirable to get away from these controls. I have noticed the Minister of Munitions and Supply is dropping some of them. I believe the committee in question is the only one of its kind; there is no other which functions in any other department of government.
I see the treasury board as a stumbling block to the wheels of progress. Many departments of government are desirous of doing certain things, but they must obtain the approval of the treasury board before they can proceed. The committee in question is a similar one. In the first instance I can well understand that it took some of the work from the then minister, and at that time it was desirable to do so. But with the machinery now developed I do not believe the committee is necessary, and I believe, further, that it now retards progress.
I have sufficient confidence in the auxiliary services, the defence organizations and the Department of National War Services to believe that they can handle the business now, without the advice of busy men like Mr. Burton, Mr. Wallace Campbell and others, whose names I shall not mention. I am thinking about the work begun by the Canadian Legion educational services, both in Canada and overseas. Many boys in the armed forces have begun work on those educational courses, but before completion of the courses they may be discharged from the services. Is there any provision whereby, in cooperation with the legion in Canada, when a man of that kind returns from overseas with a partly completed course he may pick up

War Appropriation-War Services
the work in Canada? Or, does that man go back to the supervision of the Department of Pensions and National Health, and receive further instruction through a process of rehabilitation? If he is routed in that way I believe he will be forced to lose valuable time he has already spent in study, and it is my view that his studies should be continued in Canada, through the same organization. I believe that if these studies are continued through the regular processes of rehabilitation, in other schools, much of the work done will have been wasted.
I suggest strongly to the minister that in the light of present circumstances the decision to maintain this remote-control board is one which should be reconsidered, because I believe it has outlived its usefulness and serves no purpose to-day.
Mr. LaFLECHE: At the beginning of his observations the hon. member said that some members of the board were extremely busy men. Undoubtedly that is so, and perhaps it is just another instance of the willing horse doing a large part of the work. But I have great faith in busy men of a certain calibre who accept national duties. Here we find these gentlemen .working, not for themselves, but so that they may place all their talents and abilities at the disposal of the state.
May I assure the hon. member that the board has not authority. Authority and responsibility are those of the minister. The board only recommends. The minister acts, and he is responsible for what he does. That is the way it works.
The suggestion has been made that the board should be disbanded. May I assure the hon. member that, had I not the benefit of the services of the board in question I would feel very much cut adrift. My anxiety, rather, is that some day they will tell me that the war is ending or is over, that they have other things to do and, having done their job, that they will ask to be excused. That would be my fear. I do not like to see the hon. member for Cape Breton South worrying about anything that might have an adverse effect upon members of the armed forces, as a result of the operations of this board. It is my feeling and my conviction that the members of the armed forces benefit greatly from this board, because of the kind of people who are on it.
As to members of the armed forces beginning courses overseas, and then returning to Canada, may I point out that any member in that position may pick up in Canada the threads of the course he began in Great Britain.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add just one more word to what I said this afternoon. We are dealing with the estimates having to do with the charities division, all of which comes under the charities act of September 9, 1939. The principle is that these auxiliary services will be financed from a general fund. The minister has said that this is a changing war, and it does change from year to year, from month to month and from week to week. The fifth year of the war is different from the fourth year; there are more soldiers overseas and more services are required. I understand that the practice now is for some of the charities which have been named, such as the Canadian Legion, to obtain the sanction of the minister to collect funds which are in addition to those obtained from the general fund. Then there is still another duplication. Many of these organizations go to the municipalities and obtain permission to hold tag days, and other organizations receive contributions from some of the various community efforts. There is no doubt that there is duplication in the collection of funds, but this may be explained by the fact that this is a changing war.
I come now to the' distribution of the services. There has been a change in the war since the minister dealt with this matter on July 13 last. I understand that now five or six different charities have been allocated particular work and there is no longer any duplication in this regard. The amount involved has been raised from $7,000,000 to $12,000,000, and there will have to be a further increase when we enter the sixth year of the war. We do not know when the war will close. I think the work of the department has been quite satisfactory, although I would raise the point that the public are not sufficiently informed about this matter. They know there is duplication in the collection of funds, but they do not know much about the distribution.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if his department has been able to make any calculation of the total amount collected in one way and another, not just for charitable -work but for providing goods and services to make the life of the soldier overseas a little easier. For instance, in the Chateau Laurier, and I suppose in other hotels as well, we find boxes in which people staying in the hotel can contribute to provide cigarettes for soldiers overseas or for some other purpose. The Canadian corps have a definite programme for the raising of funds and they provide many necessary supplies to our soldiers overseas. The same is true of the Canadian Legion and the Amps Association, et cetera.

War Appropriation-War Services
The Bloor street business men's association of Toronto, with which I am associated, each month sends many thousands of cigarettes overseas. In, the stores up and down Bloor street they have some sort of affair like a small lighthouse made out of cardboard into which customers place deposits. The St. Clair avenue business men's association do the same thing, as do many other associations throughout Canada. I shall not take the time to name them all but they are many in number. The women's branch of my own political organization, the Progressive Conservative Davenport-Dovercourt women's association, each year at Christmas sends an average of two hundred boxes overseas filled with goods to a value of not less than $5 each. This organization has received many interesting letters from soldiers overseas who have received these boxes.
The Montreal Star has been sponsoring a Queen Elizabeth fund which now amounts to some millions of dollars. The Toronto Evening Telegram has sponsored perhaps the greatest fund of all. This fund was started by Alderman John Innes, who came to Ottawa last evening with a Toronto city council delegation and met a number of the Toronto members this morning and during the afternoon. This fund was started two or three years ago by the alderman making the first contribution of $10. I went out a moment ago to try to get the exact amount, but I was not able to locate it.

My leader got it more quickly than I could. The editor of the Toronto Telegram, Mr. C. 0. Knowles, told me that his paper has been assisted by many newspapers in Ontario, the Orillia Packet and Times, for example. These newspapers in the smaller communities sponsor funds and the proceeds are sent to the Toronto Evening Telegram fund. I have wondered on more than one occasion whether the department sends a letter of appreciation to these newspapers in recognition of the work they are doing? Then I imagine that every church in Canada is sending regular supplies to the members who are overseas.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am glad to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Davenport in tribute to the generosity of the Canadian people. The more experience I gain, the more I deal with the Canadian public, the more I like and admire them. They are extremely generous and always respond to an honest appeal. Up to the end of the fiscal year of 1943, a little over a year ago, the total collections by the several organizations, a

number of which were mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport, amounted to $86,000,000. Returns are now coming in for the last year and are being tabulated up to March 31,
1944.	We estimate at the moment that about $26,000,000 will have been collected from a generous Canadian public for the purposes which my hon. friend has in mind.
The public organizations mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport are very well known to me and my department, and I am a hearty admirer of those who do such good work. May it be suggested that perhaps we have not yet reached the stage in this war where much public recognition can be given to many. However, records are being kept, and I do hope that when the time comes, the Canadian public will be made aware of the excellent work done by so many. I could, of course, add a number of excellent organizations to the two or three mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport. I could add the Toronto Star, the French newspapers in my own province, and the Montreal Star, which has done excellent work. I think every public service in Canada and every man connected with the Canadian public are sensitive to the necessity of doing well by their brother Canadians.
I thank the minister for mentioning the Toronto Star. If I did not mention it, I should have done so.

There are a fewr questions I should like to ask, and hon. members will pardon me if they are already familiar with these matters. As I understand it, we vote the money for these recognized war charities. Who has the control to say which of these charities shall operate in the various camps maintained by the armed services? Is it this advisory board of which we have heard so much to-day?
Then, as to the money we vote for these various organizations, who passes on the question of whether the money is properly spent? I had an opportunity of speaking to a number of persons who were at a certain camp which a certain organization was servicing, and I was told that the individual in charge of this particular service at the camp did not seem to realize the importance and the necessity of carrying on the work he was really sent there to do, whereas at another camp a similar organization was doing excellent work. No doubt the difference was due to the difference in the representatives of the organization at the two different camps. Who has control of the money that we vote? Who sees that good use is made of the money? Who inquires

War Appropriation-War Services
whether at another camp a certain organization might not be coming across with the goods, so to speak? That is something that some of us would like to know.
Again, where a camp no longer requires the number of war charities that were servicing it, who decides which organization shall pull out and which shall stay? These questions are of concern to the public. We realize that the expenditure is small in comparison with some other expenditures. Nevertheless, we would like to know how this work is carried on. Have I made myself clear to the minister?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I shall try to answer my hon. friend. The hon. member for Humboldt perhaps did not hear me this afternoon when I told the committee that each one of these projects is initiated by the department concerned, army, navy or air force. National defence makes the choice and advises me which auxiliary service shall carry on the work. If it is a canteen, that would be run by one service. If it is a hostel, that would be run by an. auxiliary service chosen by national defence, not by this department.
As to the successful operation of a project, of course much depends upon the manager or supervisor. At the beginning of the war perhaps they did not have a great many experienced supervisors, but time has seen to that and the reports I get are that the supervisors are doing a better job each year. At any rate they are followed up carefully, as in all other businesses, and there are auditors and inspectors. I hope and really believe that each one of these services is doing an excellent job.

This item is for departmental administration. I do not know under which item I should ask a question with respect to the government office of economy control which was in effect at least last year. I do not know whether it is now in effect or not. Under which item would that question Come?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Under the last item, for sundries.

This afternoon the hon, member for Vancouver South brought to the attention of the minister the desirability of educational services being made use of by the patients in our military hospitals. I understood the minister to say that he would make inquiries and let us know to what extent these services were being made available in some of our larger hospitals. I rise to inform the minister that I was told recently that these services have not been available in the Lancaster military hospital at the city of Saint John. I
was disappointed to receive this information, and I hope that situation will be corrected.
I understood the minister to say this afternoon that the application for these educational services in our hospitals had to be made through the officer commanding the hospital. If that is so, I would suggest that some change be made in the regulations, because the officer commanding, in charge of a military hospital, has a good many duties. I would suggest to the minister that officers from his department or from some other department be appointed to visit these hospitals and to point out to the military patients the opportunity they have, while there in hospital, of obtaining this education service and of the advantage it would be to them to apply themselves to some of these subjects while they are confined to the hospital.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am grateful to the hon. member for bringing this matter up again. Men in hospital could undoubtedly benefit greatly from the educational service. I told the hon. member foT Vancouver South this afternoon that I did not believe I would be able to get the information for this evening. I promised to let the committee have it; I recall that because I saw a copy of Hansard just after dinner, and I know that is there on record. We shall have to get the information; we will bring it down, and we shall also have the remarks made by my hon. friend and will see that they receive attention.

This afternoon the minister
was speaking about courses for soldiers and he said that a certain class of certificate was issued. I wish he would explain a little more fully what he means by this "class of certificate." Is it a certificate which is recognized by high schools or by the various universities in the different provinces?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I said this afternoon
that there would be given a certificate of attainment to those members of the forces who followed an educational course such as we have been discussing. I have not a copy of the certificate. I know that will be done; my hon. friend may rely on that.

Yes, but the point is, what is the benefit of this certificate of attainment? Does it entitle the soldier to a standing in a college or a high school or a university? Does it mean anything?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The certificate of attainment will have the same force in the scholastic world as a certificate from a school. If a pupil is able to show a certificate that he has attained the level of senior matriculation, that will be given credence and effect in the school which he wishes to enter. That is the plan.

War Appropriation-War Services
You cannot let these men study and then not have credit for the work which they have accomplished. When they attain a particular level of scholastic attainment it will so be certified and they will be given credit.

Could the minister give us
some idea of the number of soldiers who have attained a certificate equal to either junior or senior matriculation?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I am sorry I have not
that. This afternoon I read what I took at the time to be too many statistics. I shall get them if my hon. friend wishes it.

Does the minister know
approximately how many soldiers are taking these courses?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	My hon. friend will find
that in Hansard. Would my hon. friend say what information he wants to get, and I will see that he gets it.

The approximate number of soldiers who are taking these various courses.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Again, for fear of making an error I do not wish to make any statement, because I am not absolutely certain. I gave the figures this afternoon.

That is all right. Just one further question so that there will be no misunderstanding. I take it from what the minister says that these certificates of attainment will be recognized by any school or college in any province of Canada, and that if a soldier obtains a certificate of attainment in England equivalent to senior matriculation, that certificate would entitle him then to enter Toronto university or any other university in Canada?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes; I have that information in my book, and it comes from the authorities. That is exactly what I take it to be, and it is in that light that I gave this information to the committee.

I want to be sure it is not
just an opinion that the minister is giving, but that he knows definitely that this certificate will be recognized and accepted.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have been advised that such will be the case, and I have not the slightest reason to disbelieve what I have been told. Whether the course takes place overseas or here, it has the same value.

Item agreed to.
Salvage division, $310,750.

Will the minister give us some details of this particular expenditure? There are probably three main portions of

it, namely, salaries, travelling expenses and publicity. Would he give us particulars of the publicity angle of it?
Mr. LaFLECHE: My hon. friend will have noted that there is a decrease of $86,215 as compared with last year. The break-down of the total for the present fiscal year which I am now submitting to the committee is $310,750, composed of: salaries, $90,000; cost of living bonus, $3,500; unemployment insurance, $250; travelling expenses, $53,000; printing and stationery, $4,000; publicity, $150,000; miscellaneous, $10,000.

Has the minister the figures indicating the manner in which that $150,000 for publicity is spent?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The item of $150,000 for publicity makes provision, of course, for the maximum we anticipate having to spend for that purpose. Our experience in dealing with salvage has been that it is impossible to estimate in advance exactly what may happen in that field during the coming year. To illustrate, may I say that, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1944, we had earmarked $250,000 for publicity but we spent only about $37,000; we found it possible to carry out the work without spending the money. We were very fortunate in the last year in getting a vast amount of contributed advertising. There are several firms in Canada who patriotically gave salvage the advantage of their sponsorship in the papers, in the public press, and on the radio. The. time will come when I shall be in a position to express thanks to those several firms for the outstanding contributions which they have made. It was not necessary for me as minister to take steps to spend more than a relatively small amount out of the quarter of a million dollars voted for publicity last year. That item is $100,000 less this year than it was last year. We are very careful in spending money on publicity and other things. I hope, and I believe, that $150,000 will be enough. I hope that it will be. too much and that we shall not have to spend it all.

That is surprising to me because the figures that are given on page 397 of Hansard for last year are $396,965. Does the minister say that that money was not spent?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I was speaking of the item for publicity.

Yes, I know.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Last year that item was $250,000. The figure now before the committee is $150,000. I explained that last year

War Appropriation-War Services
we spent $38,000 out of $250,000. I explained why it was possible to save a very great deal of money.

How much was spent by the department altogether last year on salvage?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The books have not yet been closed, but the last recorded expenditures that I have are $171,975.

That is the total?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes; it will be more than that, but that is a very large part of the expenditure.

What it means is that last year the publicity was down considerably from what it was the year before?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes.

Because the year before it was $146,000.
Mr. LaFLECHE: That is correct.

That has been reduced to $38,000?
Mr. LaFLECHE: It was possible to achieve the results without spending the people's money.

The point I am making is this: What is the difference between the $146,000 spent the year before and the $38,000 spent last year? Why should there be such a large spread? How was it the government could save so much money in the two years?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I began by explaining that it has been borne upon me through observations that it is not possible to judge clearly and correctly in advance the game of salvage. In the last fiscal year the department was very fortunate. It was able to fill every demand made upon it, I am extremely happy to say, and we did so at very little expense. For instance, one decides to advertise in an acute emergency. After having tried all other attempts, one then is driven to go to paid advertising. Last year that was not necessary. At the present moment we are faced with an acute shortage of waste paper. We have had inestimable benefit from certain generous sponsors. Since some paper mills may be forced to close down I am now considering with the officials of my department and with the other departments of government in close touch with the paper industry the getting out of a campaign of advertising to cost somewhere around $60,000. Despite all the assistance we have had we are not satisfied that we have safeguarded the position sufficiently.
In order to make sure we are going to do some advertising. That will come, of course, out of the $100,000.

Could the minister give us an indication of the amount of revenue that was obtained last year as a result of the salvage campaign?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I must explain that the department cannot claim that all the results of its salvage campaigns are reported to the department, because while the urge to save secondary materials or salvage materials may be very great, yet the persons who save and turn in waste materials may do so through channels which do not report. The department does not say that they must turn in their salvage to certain people or certain firms. What the department does is to promote and bring the Canadian public to the point of finding the materials which we absolutely need if we are to carry on our full war effort. Nevertheless we have in dollars a figure well over $3,000,000 in value.

For what period?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Since May 1, 1941. That figure comes up only to last year. We know the value of salvage materials is much greater than that, but those reports were not made to the department. When the country needs certain salvage material what we try to do is to see that the scrap iron is made available to the'mills. We want the waste paper turned in to the mills. We think about one-half of the actual salvage resulting from our campaigns come to us in the form of reports.

Was there a complete change made in the administrative set-up of the salvage campaign last year?
Mr. LaFLECHE: No. I am afraid I am taking the hon. member's question on too wide a basis. There has been no revolutionary change. There have been betterments; there have been extensions of organization where necessary adjustments were possible. Things have gone on very much the same. It is true the machine has run better because the employees and officials know their job better than they did before. Perhaps my hon. friend would ask a more precise question.

The reason I ask that question is this: in the city of Saskatoon from which I come we had an able and active association in charge of salvage. Last year at some time or another the officials came along and changed it, took it away from them and changed what I think was the whole set-up as far as salvage in Saskatoon was

concerned. I should like to know why that was done in view of the fact that this organization had charge of it from the beginning. It was the only organization that was prepared to take it over from the beginning. I should like to know whether the same attitude was taken in other communities where organizations had taken on salvage campaigns and had made a success of it. Did the administration or administrative officials come along and change the whole set-up?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I understand that the case mentioned by my hon. friend was that of a voluntary committee and that there were changes; but the changes came from within the membership of the voluntary committee. My hon. friend shakes his head.

I know they did not.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I can only repeat the instructions I am given. Perhaps my hon. friend would help me by giving some further information which might be of assistance.	*

All I can say is that this association was carrying on efficiently and adequately and that for some reason or another-that is what I wanted to find out- the officials of the department came along and said they were going to take the work away from them. Actually the fact is that when this thing was established in the first place this was the only association prepared to go in and do the work. They did an adequate job, and I thought they were treated very unfairly.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am sure my hon. friend will not mind if I say I hope he is mistaken. I do not get the story that way at all; I understand that the original chairman-moved from the city and that he was replaced. That is what I am told. However, if my hon. friend would be good enough to give me further information I shall look into the matter in the interests of all concerned.
I shall be glad to do so.

The minister is discussing the matter of salvage, and as I came in I thought I heard him say there was a great need for the collection of waste paper. Quite recently it was drawn to my attention that there has been a tremendous waste of paper at the Barriefield barracks near Kingston, and I would suggest that the minister look into the matter. The person who brought the situation to my attention was disturbed, in view of the fact that the government was
[Mr. Bence.}
spending a certain amount of money in advertising the need for saving waste paper.. I would hesitate to say now the quantity that I was told was being destroyed every day at this point, but it was very considerable. I suggest that the minister look into this matter, and also into the waste that may be going on at other military camps.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am very glad the hon. gentleman has brought this to my attention. The salvage division of my department deals with these matters through the army disposal board, and we have a committee which looks after these things. I shall look into the situation mentioned by the hon. member.

I wonder if paper salvage is still going on. Is the salvage division still collecting waste paper?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes.

I do not wish to criticize the minister at all, but I should like to show him something I brought back with me from New Westminster, which has caused me a great deal of concern. The people out there are asking why we should be trying to conserve paper on the one hand, while on the other hand people who cannot get enough paper for their requirements are asked to display large posters such as the one I am holding up. The person who gave me this said, "The government will have to supply me with a new wall on which to hang it." Here is a paper poster which would cost probably fifty cents; these are sent out from Ottawa by the ton, no doubt. I should like the minister to look into this matter, though I realize that it does not come under his department. It seems to me, however, that his efforts in regard to salvage are being sabotaged, at least as far as paper is concerned.
My particular reason for rising at this time is that I have found that many departments here in Ottawa pay no attention at all to the criticism made by a member of parliament outside the House of Commons. I feel so keenly about this matter that I made up my mind that when the proper time came I would bring it to the attention of the appropriate minister in the hope that the officials responsible for the production and distribution of posters of this kind might be told that there is a scarcity of paper, and that they should consider the cost of preparing and sending out things of this kind. I feel sure this poster would weigh almost a pound. The man who gave it to me has had his own paper supply cut by some twenty-five per cent. He said, "I cannot obtain paper; I am put on a quota; yet I am asked to place a poster like this on my wall." He gave me at least half a dozen

War Appropriation-War Services
of these posters, though they were not all the same size. The minister is not to blame, of course, but I want to show that his efforts in regard to paper salvage are being sabotaged by other government departments which are not giving him the cooperation I think he should have.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have taken note of the advertisement in question, though of course it does not come under my department. This deals with a very difficult question, in regard to which the interest of Canadians must be aroused without fail. As regards the departments in Ottawa, I am very happy to say that they have gone in for a combined, well coordinated, well backed up waste-paper salvage campaign. I am in touch with a committee on which each department is represented, and as far as salvage is concerned I think the results will be better this spring than at any time in the past.
I can send them these posters; I have plenty of them.

Has the minister been given full cooperation by the various manufacturing plants throughout the country? I ask this question because I had occasion to bring to the attention of the management of one organization the fact that several tons of paper in the form of cartons and things like that were being burned every day or so. That was not a very good example for the men in the plant. As soon as the situation was made known to the management the matter was attended to and the paper saved. I wonder if there is close cooperation between the salvage branch and the various manufacturing concerns in Canada so that much of the paper that has been destroyed in the past may be saved in future.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I have mentioned already the salvage operations being conducted by the various departments of government. Within the last months the usual collections of waste paper have been more than doubled, and any increase of one hundred per cent is a good increase. Through the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, boards of trade, chambers of commerce, trade papers and so on we hope within a short time to increase the usual tonnage of waste paper collected throughout Canada by about 150 per cent. I must say that we have the finest of cooperation from the associations I have just mentioned. For instance, a trade paper called the "Drug Merchandiser" has shown the greatest of generosity. They have appealed to the druggists of Canada to make certain to save the waste material-waste paper-and turn it into the regular trade channels, so that 100-146
